message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of tasks:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from operating systems to office apps. | Specialized for parallel processing – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32) with powerful control logic, large caches, and complex pipelines. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores optimized for executing the same instruction on many data elements simultaneously. |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex, capable of branching, caching, and handling diverse workloads. | Simpler, often SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) – great for repetitive math operations. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth memory access, sophisticated prefetching. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies on massive shared memory and high‑bandwidth memory buses. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Sequential tasks, decision making, I/O bound processes. | Parallelizable tasks like matrix multiplication, image/video processing, neural network inference/training. |
| **Performance** | Optimized for low latency on single threads. | Optimized for throughput on many threads. |
| **Energy Efficiency** | Higher power consumption per core due to complexity. | Lower power per core, but many cores can still consume significant power overall. |

In short, CPUs excel at tasks that require quick, varied instructions and low latency, while GPUs shine when you can run the same operation over many data points at once, delivering high throughput.
